sm: The hosts introduce a Black Friday edition of Morning Wire, noting a recent economic roller coaster of lower gas prices, stock market scares, and tech outages. They talk with Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics and trade at the Cato Institute. Asked why Democrats made gains in the midterms despite Republican claims of economic gains, he says voters are still angry about the cost of living, which began with historically high inflation under the Biden administration. Voters wanted outright deflation, and tariffs and the Iran war have pushed up prices for goods, energy, and fertilizer. On holiday spending, he cautions against reading too much into it, since consumers have kept spending regardless of who is president. He adds that nominal figures can hide flat spending once inflation is factored in, meaning Americans are mostly treading water.

Lincicome says outages at payment systems or big retail sites could depress spending a bit, but most Christmas lists are already set, so much of the delayed spending would simply happen a week or so later. On the stock market, he describes near-daily wild swings after the election and the Nvidia scandal. Stocks are still up significantly over several years, but large declines can hurt consumer spending through the wealth effect, particularly among retirees. If the gyrations continue through winter, they will probably temper spending and growth somewhat. On gas prices, he says the main driver is supply and demand: more crude was already leaving the Gulf region before the election, and that supply is now working through refineries. Prices remain higher than a year and a half ago, and holiday travel raises them only briefly compared with summer.

Looking at the new Democratic members of Congress, he expects a focus on affordability, especially tariff reform, since Americans link tariffs to higher living costs. Democrats will also pursue oversight of Trump deals and the administration's equity stakes in private companies. The effect on economic policy will be limited, though, because a presidential veto would need two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override. Asked what is underreported, he points to a sustained rise in business formation over the last two years, which he ties to the AI boom. AI makes legal documents, tax preparation, and regulatory compliance easier, so more people are starting their own businesses. The hosts agree it empowers individuals and thank him.
